# From Numbers to Grease: The Accountant Powering Vehicles with Vegetable Oil

By day, Josh Winston crunches numbers as a professional accountant, meticulously balancing ledgers and ensuring financial accuracy for his clients. But when the workday ends, Winston trades his calculator for a wrench, pursuing a passion project that has evolved into a unique side business: converting vehicles to run on vegetable oil instead of traditional diesel fuel.

Winston's journey into alternative fuel conversion began four years ago, sparked by an unlikely source—a late-night news segment exploring the growing trend of vegetable oil conversions. Intrigued by the possibility of powering vehicles with a renewable, often recycled resource, Winston decided to investigate further. His curiosity quickly turned into action when he purchased a $900 conversion kit, taking his first tentative steps into what would become a consuming hobby and eventual business venture.

His initial foray into the world of vegetable oil conversion proved successful when he converted a truck, demonstrating that the technology could work in practice, not just theory. Encouraged by this achievement, Winston expanded his efforts to his own 1998 Jetta. The conversion proved so effective that the car became something of a local curiosity—thanks in large part to a bumper sticker Winston affixed to the vehicle, boldly advertising its unconventional fuel source. The sticker sparked countless conversations and questions from curious onlookers, fellow drivers, and passersby who were fascinated by the idea of a car running on vegetable oil rather than fossil fuels.

This growing interest eventually inspired Winston to formalize his hobby into a business, which he named "Feed My Wheels dot com." According to Winston, his venture holds the distinction of being the only service of its kind in the greater Washington, D.C. area—a notable claim given the increasing interest in sustainable and alternative fuel solutions. Despite this unique market position, Winston's business remains relatively small in scale, having completed conversions on only a handful of vehicles to date. Nevertheless, the niche nature of his work has allowed him to carve out a distinctive reputation among those seeking eco-friendly transportation alternatives.

Winston's most recent and ambitious undertaking pushed the boundaries of his expertise even further: the conversion of a 1983 Itasca RV. This project represented a significant step up in complexity from his previous conversions, requiring him to adapt his methods to accommodate the larger vehicle and its more demanding power requirements. The process was far from smooth sailing, as Winston encountered numerous technical challenges along the way. He grappled with persistently dead batteries that required troubleshooting and replacement, as well as a faulty alternator that complicated the RV's electrical system. Through persistent trial and error, Winston worked through these obstacles, drawing on the problem-solving skills he's honed both in his accounting career and his years of hands-on conversion experience.

Despite the challenges, Winston's dedication to his unconventional side business reflects a broader commitment to sustainable transportation solutions, proving that with enough determination—and perhaps a bit of stubbornness—even complex mechanical projects can be tackled by those willing to learn as they go.

# From Spreadsheets to Salvaged Vegetable Oil: One Man's Journey Into Alternative Fuel

Josh Winston never imagined that a career in accounting would lead him to spend his weekends elbow-deep in fryer grease, running fuel lines through a thirty-year-old motorhome. But that's exactly where his life has taken him since a chance encounter with a late-night news segment changed everything.

It was an ordinary evening when Winston, then working a standard nine-to-five as an accountant, stumbled across a short television feature about vehicles that could run on used vegetable oil instead of traditional diesel fuel. The segment showed enthusiasts collecting spent cooking oil from restaurants, filtering it, and pouring it into modified fuel tanks—essentially turning waste into a viable, low-cost fuel source. For most viewers, it might have been a passing curiosity. For Winston, it sparked an obsession.

"I couldn't stop thinking about it," he has said of that initial spark of interest. "The idea that you could take something restaurants were literally throwing away and use it to power a vehicle—it seemed almost too simple to be true."

What began as idle curiosity soon turned into hands-on experimentation. Winston started researching diesel engine conversions, studying how vegetable oil's different viscosity and combustion properties required specific modifications—typically a secondary fuel tank, a heating element to thin the oil, and a switching mechanism to start and stop the engine on regular diesel. He began tinkering with his own vehicles, learning through trial and error, online forums, and the small but passionate community of grease-car enthusiasts scattered across the country.

Eventually, his hobby evolved into something more formal. Winston launched "Feed My Wheels dot com," a small business based in the Washington, D.C. area dedicated to converting diesel vehicles to run on used vegetable oil. Word spread slowly at first, mostly through word-of-mouth and online communities interested in sustainable living and alternative fuels. Clients ranged from environmentally conscious commuters looking to cut fuel costs to hobbyists eager to join the same movement that had once captivated Winston himself.

## The Itasca Challenge

Among all the vehicles Winston has worked on, none has tested his skills—or his patience—quite like a 1983 Itasca RV, which stands as his largest and most ambitious conversion project to date. Unlike smaller cars and trucks, the RV's scale introduced a host of complications that pushed Winston's expertise to its limits.

The project was plagued by mechanical setbacks from the start. Dead batteries left the vehicle stranded more than once during the conversion process, forcing Winston to troubleshoot electrical systems that had aged along with the rest of the RV. Alternator problems compounded the difficulty, requiring additional repairs before he could even begin focusing on the vegetable oil conversion itself. And, in a mishap that has become something of a rite of passage among grease-car converters, oil spills during the installation process added a messy, frustrating layer to an already complex job.

Despite the setbacks, Winston pressed on, viewing each obstacle as part of the learning curve that comes with working on unconventional, alternative-fuel projects. The Itasca, with its aging systems and sheer size, became a testament to both the challenges and the rewards of this kind of work—proof that patience and persistence could transform even a decades-old motorhome into a functioning example of sustainable engineering.

## A Niche But Growing Movement

Winston's work sits within a small but dedicated subculture of alternative-fuel enthusiasts across the United States. By some estimates, fewer than 10,000 vehicles nationwide have been converted to run on used vegetable oil or similar alternative fuels—a tiny fraction compared to the millions of conventional vehicles on American roads. Yet for those involved, the appeal goes beyond mere novelty.

For many enthusiasts, the draw lies in reducing dependence on fossil fuels, cutting fuel costs by using oil that would otherwise be discarded, and embracing a do-it-yourself ethos that values ingenuity and environmental responsibility over convenience. Restaurants often give away used cooking oil for free, since disposal can otherwise be a costly hassle for them, creating a mutually beneficial arrangement between businesses and grease-car owners.

Still, the practice comes with real challenges. Vehicles must be properly converted with the right equipment, oil must be carefully filtered to remove food particles and water, and drivers must adjust to routines like switching between diesel and vegetable oil depending on engine temperature. Mechanical issues—like those Winston encountered with the Itasca—are not uncommon, particularly in older vehicles where multiple systems may already be nearing the end of their lifespan.

Despite these hurdles, Winston has continued to grow his business, drawn by the same fascination that first hooked him after watching that news segment years ago. What started as a hobby rooted in curiosity has become a small but meaningful contribution to a niche movement—one spilled tank of oil, one dead battery, and one converted vehicle at a time.

Bethesda, Maryland, is an affluent unincorporated community located in Montgomery County, just northwest of Washington, D.C. Known for its vibrant downtown area, upscale shopping districts, and proximity to the nation's capital, Bethesda has become home to numerous corporate headquarters and federal agencies, including the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the Discovery, Inc. headquarters (formerly Discovery Communications).

The connection to CNN comes through corporate ownership structures in the media industry. Discovery, Inc., which was headquartered in Bethesda for many years, merged with WarnerMedia in 2022 to form Warner Bros. Discovery. This merger brought CNN—one of the world's most recognized cable news networks—under the same corporate umbrella as Discovery's portfolio of channels, which was managed from its Bethesda offices before the company later relocated its headquarters.

This merger represented one of the significant consolidations in the media landscape, combining Discovery's factual and lifestyle programming with WarnerMedia's entertainment assets, including HBO, Warner Bros. Pictures, and CNN's news division. The deal reflected broader trends in the media industry toward consolidation as companies sought to compete with streaming giants and diversify their content offerings.

Bethesda itself, meanwhile, continues to thrive as a business-friendly community, attracting biotechnology firms, government contractors, and corporate offices due to its strategic location near Washington, D.C., excellent public transportation via the Metro system, and high quality of life. The city's evolution into a corporate hub illustrates how suburban communities near major metropolitan areas can become significant players in national industries, even when the household names associated with those industries—like CNN—are more commonly associated with other cities such as Atlanta, where CNN's news operations are primarily based.

# From Fryer to Freeway: The Mechanic Turning Fast Food Waste Into Fuel

**By the time most people finish their morning coffee, Mike Delgado has already made his rounds to three restaurants, collecting five-gallon buckets of used cooking oil that would otherwise end up in a landfill.**

"People think I'm crazy when they see me pull up to the back of a Chinese takeout place in a truck that smells like French fries," Delgado says, laughing as he hoists a bucket into the bed of his converted 2006 Ford F-250. "But this truck runs cleaner than most cars twice its age."

Delgado, 34, runs a small conversion shop out of a converted barn in rural Oregon, where he transforms diesel engines to run on waste vegetable oil (WVO) — the same grease restaurants use to cook french fries, chicken wings, and doughnuts. Instead of paying to dispose of it, eateries hand it over to Delgado for free.

"It's a win-win," he says. "They save on disposal fees, and I get fuel that costs me almost nothing."

## An Unlikely Path to Grease

Delgado didn't set out to become a biofuel pioneer. A former auto shop teacher, he stumbled into the world of vegetable oil conversions after watching a documentary about sustainable living nearly a decade ago.

"I thought it was a gimmick at first," he admits. "Then I did the math. Diesel engines were basically designed to run on peanut oil — Rudolf Diesel showed that off back in 1900. We just forgot."

After building his first conversion kit for his own truck, friends started asking him to do the same for theirs. Word spread through local farming communities, then further, as social media picked up his story. Today, Delgado has converted more than 200 vehicles — trucks, vans, even an old school bus that now shuttles kids to a summer camp.

## How It Works

The process isn't as simple as pouring old grease into a gas tank, Delgado is quick to clarify.

"Straight vegetable oil is thick, like syrup, especially when it's cold," he explains. "You need a heating system so it flows properly, and a second tank so the engine can start on regular diesel, then switch over once it warms up."

His conversion kits include a secondary fuel tank, heating elements, and filtration systems that strip out food particles before the oil ever reaches the engine. A full setup costs customers between $1,200 and $2,000 — a fraction of the cost of an electric vehicle, he notes, and with a much smaller environmental footprint than manufacturing a new battery-powered car.

"You're not creating new demand for oil. You're recycling something that already exists," Delgado says. "That grease was going to get dumped anyway."

## More Than Just a Mechanic

For Delgado, the work is as much about community as it is about combustion engines.

Local restaurant owner Trần Thị Hoa, who runs a noodle shop in nearby Ashland, says Delgado's visits have saved her hundreds of dollars a year in oil disposal costs.

"Before, we had to pay someone to haul it away," she says. "Now Mike comes, takes it, and even brings us vegetables from his garden sometimes. It feels good knowing it's not wasted."

Delgado has also mentored several young mechanics through informal apprenticeships, teaching them the trade for free in exchange for help around the shop.

"There's not a lot of jobs like this left," says 19-year-old apprentice Casey Lund, who dropped out of community college to work with Delgado. "He's teaching me stuff you can't learn from YouTube videos — real hands-on knowledge."

## The Open Road Smells Like Popcorn

Despite the growing interest in electric vehicles, Delgado believes there's still a place for his particular brand of ingenuity — one rooted in resourcefulness rather than reinvention.

"I'm not anti-electric. I think we need all kinds of solutions," he says. "But not everyone can afford a $40,000 EV. Some people just have an old diesel truck sitting around, and a little creativity can turn it into something surprisingly green."

As for the smell — something Delgado says he's asked about constantly — it depends on what type of oil his customers have been collecting.

"Sometimes it smells like doughnuts. Sometimes it's like driving behind a Chinese restaurant," he says. "Either way, people are always hungry by the time they get where they're going."

# The Numbers Guy Who Runs on Vegetable Oil

**By day, he balances ledgers. By night, he's converting diesel engines to run on discarded fryer grease—and building a following that has nothing to do with taxes.**

---MARIETTA, GA — Dale Fenwick spends his mornings the way you'd expect a certified public accountant to spend them: hunched over spreadsheets, reconciling quarterly filings for a roster of small businesses that includes a landscaping company, two dental practices, and a regional chain of tire shops. His office smells like toner and burnt coffee.

His afternoons smell like French fries.

That's when Fenwick, 52, trades his button-down for a stained canvas apron and walks out back to the converted pole barn he calls "the shop," where a 1998 Ford F-250 sits mid-transformation, its fuel lines exposed like a patient on an operating table. Fenwick is installing a two-tank conversion system that will let the truck's owner run on waste vegetable oil collected from restaurants around Cobb County.

"People hear 'accountant' and picture someone who color-codes their sock drawer," Fenwick said, wiping his hands on a rag that had clearly given up on being clean months ago. "Which, fair. But I also think in systems. An engine's just another kind of system. So is a fryer full of used oil nobody wants. I just figured out how to connect them."

## From Spreadsheets to Straight Vegetable Oil

Fenwick's business, Grease Monkey Conversions, started nine years ago as what he calls "a very expensive hobby that got out of hand." He'd read about straight vegetable oil (SVO) conversions online, bought a kit for his own diesel pickup, and spent a winter troubleshooting it in his garage while his wife, Renee, wondered aloud whether he'd lost his mind.

"I did wonder," Renee Fenwick confirmed, laughing. "He'd come inside smelling like a Waffle House. But then neighbors started asking him to do their trucks. Then someone with an RV showed up. It just kept going."

The technical premise is straightforward, even if the execution isn't: diesel engines, with modification, can run on filtered waste vegetable oil instead of (or alongside) traditional diesel fuel. Fenwick's conversions typically involve adding a second fuel tank, a heating element to thin the oil so it flows properly, and a switching system that starts and stops the engine on regular diesel to keep the lines clear.

He now converts eight to twelve vehicles a year — trucks, vans, and, increasingly, RVs owned by retirees looking to cut fuel costs on cross-country trips.

"The RV crowd is my bread and butter now," Fenwick said. "You've got folks on fixed incomes wanting to see the country, and diesel prices doing what diesel prices do. I tell them: find a diner, ask if you can take their old fry oil, and suddenly you're driving to Yellowstone for free."

## The Accountant's Advantage

Fenwick insists his two seemingly unrelated professions share more than people assume.

"Every job I do, I'm managing inputs and outputs," he said. "In accounting, it's dollars. In the shop, it's BTUs and viscosity. Same brain, different units."

Clients say that precision shows. Mark Delgado, a retired firefighter who had Fenwick convert his Dodge Ram three years ago, says the appeal wasn't just savings — it was trusting the person doing the work.

"He documents everything," Delgado said. "Maintenance logs, oil-filtering schedules, cost breakdowns down to the penny per mile. It's like getting an accountant's audit of your fuel system. Which, I guess, is literally what it is."

Fenwick charges by the job, with conversions typically running $1,500 to $4,000 depending on the vehicle and system complexity. He's upfront that it's not a moneymaker on the scale of his accounting practice — "I'd need to charge triple what I do to make shop rate here worthwhile" — but says that's not really the point.

"My accounting income supports my grease habit," he said. "That's just the honest math."

## Not Without Skeptics

The conversions aren't universally beloved. Mechanics unfamiliar with the systems sometimes warn customers off them, citing clogged injectors or voided warranties. Fenwick doesn't dispute the risks — he requires clients to sign a lengthy disclosure — but says most failures come from impatience, not the technology itself.

"You have to filter the oil properly. You have to let the engine warm up before switching over. People want to treat it like a magic trick instead of a process," he said. "It's not free energy. It's recycled energy. There's a difference, and it requires respect."

Environmental scientists offer measured praise. "SVO conversions are a niche solution, but they're a legitimate one for reducing waste-stream oil and offsetting some diesel demand," said Priya Anand, a sustainability researcher at Georgia Tech who has studied small-scale biofuel adoption. "The bigger impact is often the mindset shift — people start thinking about where their energy comes from."

## A Man of Two Ledgers

Back in the pole barn, Fenwick tightens a fitting on the F-250's second tank and glances at the clock. He has a client call at 4 p.m. — a bakery owner anxious about first-quarter estimated taxes.

"I'll go inside, wash the grease off my hands, and talk about depreciation schedules like everything's normal," he said. "Because it is normal. It's just my normal."

He's not sure his two worlds will ever fully make sense to outsiders. He's stopped trying to explain it and started just doing both.

"Some guys golf. Some guys fish," Fenwick said. "I balance books and I convert trucks to run on old fry oil. It's a weird combination, sure. But at the end of the day, both jobs are about taking something messy and making it work."

*Grease Monkey Conversions operates out of Marietta, Georgia, by appointment.*

# The Grease Guru of Bethesda

**BETHESDA, Md.** — In a nondescript garage tucked behind a strip mall on Old Georgetown Road, the air smells like a diner at closing time — a mix of French fries and diesel fuel. This is where Danny Reyes spends his days, elbow-deep in engines, converting ordinary diesel vehicles into machines that run on used vegetable oil.

"People think I'm running some kind of mad scientist operation back here," Reyes said, wiping his hands on a rag stained the color of weak coffee. "But it's really just plumbing. Really greasy plumbing."

Reyes, 47, founded Beltway Biofuel Conversions eight years ago after a mid-life career pivot that he describes as "equal parts environmental guilt and stubbornness." A former IT consultant, he says he converted his own pickup truck in 2016 after watching a documentary about landfill waste, and never looked back.

"I put in probably 200 hours figuring out my own truck through trial and error," he said. "Half my neighbors thought I'd lost it. My wife included."

Now, his business converts roughly 40 to 50 vehicles a year — mostly older diesel trucks and vans — installing secondary fuel tanks and heating systems that allow the vehicles to run on filtered waste vegetable oil, often sourced directly from restaurants.

The process, Reyes explained, isn't as simple as pouring in leftover fryer oil. Vehicles need a conversion kit that includes a second fuel tank, additional fuel lines, and a heat exchange system, since vegetable oil is too viscous to combust properly when cold. Drivers start the engine on regular diesel, switch over to vegetable oil once the engine warms up, and then switch back to diesel before shutting off, to keep oil from congealing in the lines.

"It's not a gimmick," he said. "These trucks run hundreds of thousands of miles on this stuff. I've got customers who haven't bought a gallon of diesel in years."

One of those customers is Marcus Webb, a landscaper from Rockville who had his box truck converted three years ago.

"I was skeptical as hell," Webb said. "I thought it was going to smell like a McDonald's parking lot everywhere I went. It really doesn't — not much, anyway. Sometimes if you're right behind me you catch a whiff of popcorn, weirdly."

Webb estimates he's saved more than $6,000 in fuel costs since the conversion, largely because he sources his oil for free from a few local restaurants that are happy to have someone haul away their waste grease.

"They used to pay someone to take it away," Webb said. "Now I take it for nothing, filter it myself, and Danny's rig does the rest."

Reyes said building relationships with restaurants is often the hardest part for new converts — not everyone wants to deal with buckets of used oil, and not every restaurant is willing to hand it over informally. Some diners have exclusive contracts with grease-collection companies that turn waste oil into biodiesel commercially, closing off that supply chain for backyard converters.

"I tell people, before you even think about the conversion, go find your oil supply first," he said. "I've seen people spend $3,000 on a kit and then have no idea where they're getting their fuel."

The business has not been without setbacks. Reyes recalls one early customer whose fuel lines clogged on a January morning because the vehicle had switched over to vegetable oil too soon, before the engine had fully warmed.

"He called me from the side of 270, engine dead, and he was not happy," Reyes said, laughing now at the memory. "I drove out with a heat gun and basically had to defrost his fuel line on the shoulder of the highway. Lesson learned — for both of us."

Despite the occasional roadside emergency, Reyes insists the technology is reliable when installed and maintained correctly, and he sees growing interest from customers motivated as much by economics as environmentalism.

"Diesel prices spike, and my phone starts ringing," he said. "People don't always care about saving the planet. Sometimes they just want to stop giving all their money to the gas station."

Still, he acknowledges the niche nature of his trade. Vegetable oil conversions remain a small corner of the alternative fuel world, overshadowed by the rise of electric vehicles. Reyes doesn't see that as a threat, exactly, but he's realistic about his business's ceiling.

"I'm never going to convert a Tesla," he said, grinning. "But there's always going to be some guy with an old diesel truck who wants to stick it to the pump. That's my customer."

For now, Reyes said he has no plans to expand beyond his single-bay operation, content instead to keep doing the work himself, one fryer-oil-scented engine at a time.

"I like keeping it small," he said. "Every truck that comes through here, I want to know it inside and out. That's not really a business plan. That's just how I like to work."

# From Backyard Experiment to Booming Business: How One Man's Curiosity Sparked a Veggie Oil Revolution

*By Staff Correspondent*

BOISE, Idaho — When Marcus Chen poured his first batch of used fryer oil into a modified diesel engine in his garage seven years ago, he wasn't trying to start a business. He was trying to prove a point to his skeptical brother-in-law during a Thanksgiving argument about gas prices.

"I said, 'You can literally run a car on french fry grease,' and he laughed at me," Chen recalled, standing in what is now a 12,000-square-foot conversion facility on the outskirts of Boise. "So I went home and figured out how to actually do it."

That stubborn streak turned into Cascade Biofuel Conversions, a company that has since retrofitted more than 800 diesel vehicles to run on waste vegetable oil (WVO) and now employs 14 people. Chen's journey — from curious hobbyist to small business owner — mirrors a quiet but persistent movement of alternative fuel enthusiasts across the country who are betting that yesterday's cooking grease is tomorrow's fuel source.

## The Learning Curve

Chen's early experiments were, by his own admission, "a mess." His first conversion kit, cobbled together from online forum instructions and mismatched parts, caused his 1998 Volkswagen Jetta to sputter and stall in a grocery store parking lot.

"I had grease literally dripping out of places it shouldn't have been," he said. "My wife was convinced I was going to burn the house down."

Undeterred, Chen spent nights and weekends researching fuel viscosity, heating systems, and filtration methods. The science, it turned out, was more forgiving than the execution: vegetable oil is thicker than diesel, especially in cold weather, so vehicles need a secondary heated fuel tank and switching system to warm the oil before it reaches the engine.

By his third attempt, the Jetta ran — reliably, and almost entirely on grease he collected for free from a local diner.

## From Hobby to Livelihood

Word spread through local car enthusiast forums and a regional Facebook group dedicated to alternative fuels. Chen began fielding requests from strangers willing to pay for his expertise. He converted his second vehicle, then a neighbor's truck, then a dozen more.

"I was doing this on nights and weekends while working a full-time job in IT," he said. "Eventually the math stopped making sense to keep doing both."

In 2019, Chen quit his corporate job and opened Cascade Biofuel Conversions with savings and a small business loan. Today, the company installs conversion kits ranging from $1,200 to $3,500 depending on vehicle complexity, and maintains partnerships with over 30 restaurants that supply used cooking oil — for free — in exchange for hauling it away.

"Restaurants used to pay rendering companies to take this stuff off their hands," Chen said. "Now we do it for nothing, and everybody wins."

## Not Without Skeptics

The alternative fuel conversion industry remains a niche corner of the automotive world, and it has its critics. Some mechanics warn that WVO conversions can void manufacturer warranties and, if done improperly, damage fuel injectors over time. Environmental researchers note that while burning used cooking oil reduces reliance on virgin diesel, the vehicles still emit particulates and aren't a wholesale climate solution.

Chen doesn't dispute the limitations.

"I'm not out here saying this saves the planet single-handedly," he said. "But it's one more way to not throw away something useful, and to give people options besides the pump."

He's also quick to note that his customers aren't ideologues. They're a mix of environmentalists, truckers looking to cut fuel costs, and self-described "tinkerers" who simply enjoy the mechanical puzzle of it.

## A Community of Believers

On a recent Saturday, Chen's shop doubled as a meeting space for the Idaho Grease Car Collective, a loose network of about 60 enthusiasts who trade tips, spare parts, and driving routes optimized around restaurants with reliable oil supplies.

Among them was Denise Whitfield, a retired schoolteacher who had Chen convert her pickup truck two years ago.

"I spend maybe $40 a month on fuel now," Whitfield said. "And I like knowing my truck runs on something that would've ended up in a landfill."

For Chen, moments like these — a room full of people who once thought his backyard experiments were a novelty — are the real payoff.

"My brother-in-law drives one of my converted trucks now," he added, smiling. "He still won't admit he was wrong. But he fills up on grease, not diesel."

# The Grease Monkey's Magnum Opus: One Man's Quest to Power a 30-Foot RV on Waste Fry Oil

**PORTLAND, Ore.** — There's a smell that follows Dale Hutchins wherever he goes. It's not unpleasant, exactly—somewhere between a state fair funnel cake stand and a mechanic's garage—but it announces his arrival before his 1983 Fleetwood Bounder ever rounds the corner.

"People think I'm hauling a food truck," Hutchins says, wiping his hands on a rag that has seen better decades. "Then this thing the size of a small house rolls up, and they get real confused."

Hutchins, 58, a semi-retired HVAC technician with the patient demeanor of a man who has been electrocuted more times than he'd like to admit, has spent the last four years converting his aging motorhome—which he's named the *Kernel Sanders*—to run on waste vegetable oil scavenged from local restaurants. It is, by his own estimation, "the dumbest, most expensive, most satisfying thing I have ever done."

## The Genesis of a Grease-Powered Dream

The idea began, as many terrible ideas do, with a documentary and two beers. Hutchins watched a segment on biodiesel conversions and became fixated on a bigger question: if a Volkswagen Jetta could run on discarded cooking oil, why not something the size of a shipping container?

"Everybody does the little diesel Rabbit conversion," he says. "I wanted to do something absurd. Go big or go home. Except the whole point was that I *am* home. It's an RV."

The math, on paper, seemed almost virtuous. Restaurants pay to have used fryer oil hauled away. Hutchins would take it for free, filter it, and burn it instead of diesel. Lower emissions, zero fuel cost, and a delightful French-fry aroma trailing behind him on the highway. What could go wrong?

Nearly everything, as it turned out.

## The Great Waffle House Incident

The first major mishap involved a 55-gallon drum of oil sourced from a regional waffle chain, which Hutchins now refers to only as "the syrup batch." Unbeknownst to him, the oil had been used to fry something involving a sugary glaze, and when it hit his converted fuel system, it behaved less like combustible liquid and more like amber-colored concrete.

"The fuel lines gummed up somewhere around Bend," he recalls. "I'm sitting on the shoulder of Highway 97, engine's dead, and there's this faint smell of maple syrup coming from under the hood. A trucker pulls over to help and just starts laughing. He goes, 'Man, your engine smells like breakfast.' I wanted to die."

The syrup batch cost him three days, a new fuel filter system, and what he describes as "a small but permanent loss of faith in the goodness of pancake houses."

## Engineering an Absurdity

The conversion itself required a two-tank system: one for conventional diesel to start and stop the engine, and a second, heated tank for the vegetable oil, which needs to be warmed to reduce its viscosity before combustion. In a car, this is a manageable engineering challenge. In a 30-foot RV with an engine bay Hutchins compares to "a game of Tetris played by someone who hates you," it became a monument to stubbornness.

He installed heat exchangers, additional filtration units, a switch panel that he wired himself ("against every recommendation from every forum I read"), and a secondary tank that he welded from an old propane tank, a decision his insurance agent still doesn't know about.

There were fires. Small ones, he's quick to clarify. "Contained fires. Learning experiences."

There was also The Great Overflow of 2021, when a valve failure sent nearly ten gallons of warm canola oil across his driveway, coating his cat, his recycling bins, and—for reasons still unexplained—a neighbor's garden gnome three properties down.

"I found grease on that gnome a week later," Hutchins says. "I don't know how. I don't want to know how."

## The Environmental Ledger

Beneath the comedy lies a genuine, if complicated, environmental argument. Waste vegetable oil, when properly filtered and burned, produces fewer particulates and a smaller net carbon contribution than fossil diesel, since the carbon released was recently absorbed by the plants the oil came from, rather than dug up from prehistoric reserves. Hutchins estimates the *Kernel Sanders* has diverted more than 900 gallons of used oil from landfills and grease traps since the project began—oil that would otherwise require costly disposal and occasionally, illegally, ends up dumped into storm drains.

"It's not a perfect solution," concedes Dr. Elena Ruiz, a sustainability researcher at Oregon State University who has followed grassroots biofuel conversions for over a decade. "You're still running a combustion engine. You still get NOx emissions, and vegetable oil combustion isn't magic—it requires energy to collect, filter, and heat the fuel. But as a form of localized waste reduction and a gateway to public conversations about fuel alternatives? These backyard projects do something policy papers can't. They make people curious."

That curiosity, Hutchins reports, mostly manifests as strangers at gas stations sniffing the air and asking if he's "cooking something back there."

## Life on the Road, Smelling Like Lunch

Despite the setbacks—the syrup incident, the gnome, an alarming incident involving a clogged line and what he describes only as "a small backfire that singed my eyebrows clean off"—Hutchins has logged over 14,000 miles in the *Kernel Sanders*, cruising through Oregon, Washington, and as far south as Northern California, trailed by a scent that has, at various points, been compared to doughnuts, egg rolls, and "Thanksgiving, somehow."

He's become something of a local celebrity at the restaurants that supply his oil, several of which now save their used fryer grease specifically for him in labeled containers—a small, greasy economy built entirely on goodwill and mutual bewilderment.

Asked if he'd do it again, Hutchins doesn't hesitate.

"Every single time," he says. "Although next time, no waffle places. Learn from my mistakes, people. Read the label. Ask about the syrup."

The *Kernel Sanders* idles in his driveway as he says this, engine humming with the unmistakable low thrum of a diesel motor and the faint, inexplicable aroma of hash browns. Somewhere down the street, presumably, a garden gnome still bears the evidence.
